items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: Threat modelling should include regular reviews and updates and address AI-specific attacks, such as data poisoning, model inversion, and membership inference.
items.why: Source of the quotation. Voluntary. Developers and operators 'shall' analyse threats; the list of AI-specific attacks is a 'should'. Provision 3.2 says threats a developer cannot resolve must be passed to operators so they can threat model their own systems, which is the basis for including bought systems. The same wording is provision 5.1.3-1 of ETSI TS 104 223 V1.1.1 (April 2025).

items.title: Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse)
items.locator: Opening section; 'No data, no instructions' and 'Developer and organisation awareness'
items.quote: Current large language models (LLMs) simply do not enforce a security boundary between instructions and data inside a prompt.
items.why: The national technical authority's explanation of why injected instructions cannot be fixed the way older injection flaws were, and why the risk must be reduced and managed rather than removed. A blog post by a named NCSC technical director, not formal guidance.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development: Secure design
items.locator: Sections 'Raise staff awareness of threats and risks' and 'Model the threats to your system'
items.quote: you apply a holistic process to assess the threats to your system
items.why: Says senior leaders should understand threats to AI, and that threat assessment covers the impact on users, organisations and wider society if an AI component is compromised, with decisions documented. Written for providers of AI systems; guidance, not a rule.

items.title: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2e2025)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Section 4.2.5 'Risk Management in Light of AML', p. 60 (PDF p. 73)
items.quote: there exist prompts that can trigger that behavior
items.why: The reference taxonomy of attacks (evasion, poisoning, privacy, prompt injection), co-authored with the UK AI Security Institute. This passage records that many defences lack provable guarantees, so testing reduces risk but does not remove it. US source; no legal force in the UK.

items.title: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
items.quote: it is unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention for prompt injection
items.why: Practitioner catalogue of the ten main risks to language-model applications; this is the first entry. Useful as a checklist of attack routes for a threat model. Community consensus document, not a standard. No publication date is shown on the page.

items.title: Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition
items.locator: Abstract on the AI Security Institute research page
items.quote: Participants submitted 1.8 million prompt-injection attacks, with over 60,000 successfully eliciting policy violations
items.why: Source of the figure: 22 frontier AI agents, 44 deployment scenarios, 1.8 million attacks, over 60,000 successes. The abstract adds that nearly all agents broke policy within 10 to 100 queries. Only the abstract on the Institute's page was read, not the full paper.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How should we assess security and data minimisation in AI?
items.locator: Sections 'What security risks does AI introduce?' and 'What types of privacy attacks apply to AI models?'
items.quote: you should stay up-to-date with the state of the art in both methods of attack and mitigation
items.why: The data protection regulator's account of model inversion, membership inference and adversarial examples, and of the security duty where personal data is processed. The page carries a banner that the guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 15: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning)
items.why: International comparator. High-risk systems must resist attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance, with measures against data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples and confidentiality attacks. Applies to high-risk systems only. The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page). The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI and the text shown is not yet updated.

items.title: Impact of AI on cyber threat from now to 2027
items.quote: almost certainly presents an increased attack surface for adversaries to exploit
items.why: The official threat assessment: building AI into the UK's technology base widens what attackers can target. Mainly about attackers using AI, so it supports the case for refreshing a threat model against current intelligence rather than describing attacks on AI in detail.

items.title: Machine learning principles: 1.2 Model the threats to your system
items.locator: Part 1: Secure design, principle 1.2, 'Why is this important?' and 'Create a high-level threat model for the ML system'
items.quote: New attacks on ML systems are demonstrated regularly, and there are significant limitations to existing defence methods.
items.why: The national technical authority's instruction to build a threat model for each machine learning system, covering what happens to the wider system if the model is attacked or fails. Version 2.0, published and reviewed 22 May 2024. Written for machine learning generally and predates most guidance on language models. Guidance, not a rule.

items.title: Cyber security risks to artificial intelligence
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Executive summary; section 4 (findings of the risk assessment); section 5 (list of case studies)
items.quote: a set of 23 case studies were identified, both real-world and theoretical proof of concepts, involving cyber-attacks linked to AI vulnerabilities
items.why: The government's commissioned map of vulnerabilities at each stage of the AI lifecycle (design, development, deployment, maintenance), separating those specific to AI from ordinary software weaknesses, with 23 attack case studies. Useful as a checklist for a threat model. Written by a consultancy and a university for the department, based on literature reviews and five client interviews; it does not rank the risks. Published May 2024, so it predates agentic systems.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 32: Security of processing
items.quote: account shall be taken in particular of the risks that are presented by processing
items.why: The one binding rule found that bears on threat awareness: when setting the level of security, a controller or processor must take account of the risks, including unlawful alteration of, disclosure of and access to personal data. It applies only where personal data is processed, is not specific to AI and does not name any AI attack. Art. 32(3) was amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

items.title: Financial Stability in Focus: Artificial intelligence in the financial system
items.publisher: Bank of England, Financial Policy Committee
items.locator: Section headed 'Changing external cyber threat environment'
items.quote: via the malicious manipulation of model training data (so-called data poisoning)
items.why: A UK financial authority naming attacks on a firm's own AI, including through suppliers and through training data, as a risk it will monitor. A statement of the Committee's view of risks to financial stability; it sets no requirement and concerns financial firms.

items.title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
items.publisher: arXiv (Greshake, Abdelnabi, Mishra, Endres, Holz and Fritz)
items.locator: Abstract on the arXiv record (version 2, 5 May 2023)
items.quote: LLM-Integrated Applications blur the line between data and instructions
items.why: The research paper that set out indirect prompt injection: instructions planted in content an assistant later retrieves, demonstrated against a live search assistant and code-completion tools. It is the origin of the attack class the NCSC blog and the NIST profile describe. Cited from the authors' preprint on arXiv; only the abstract was read, and the record itself does not state where it was peer reviewed. The products tested have since changed.

items.title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical
items.publisher: arXiv (Carlini, Jagielski, Choquette-Choo, Paleka, Pearce, Anderson, Terzis, Thomas and Tramèr)
items.locator: Abstract on the arXiv record (version 2, 6 May 2024)
items.quote: we show how we could have poisoned 0.01% of the LAION-400M or COYO-700M datasets for just $60 USD
items.why: Evidence that poisoning the public data large models are trained on is cheap and practical, not theoretical: two attacks that could have altered ten widely used datasets. The authors told the dataset maintainers and proposed defences. Cited from the authors' preprint on arXiv; only the abstract was read. It shows the attack is feasible, not how often it happens.

items.title: Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products
items.quote: LLMs amplify existing security risks and introduce new ones
items.why: What a large in-house red team learned from testing more than 100 products: eight lessons, including that the work of securing AI systems is never complete. Supports the top level of the criterion, where testing by people trying to break a system drives its design. A preprint written by one supplier's own team about its own products, not peer reviewed so far as the record shows; only the abstract was read.

items.title: Guidelines on Securing AI Systems
items.locator: Section 3 'Securing AI', opening paragraph, PDF p. 7; section 2 'Understanding AI threats', p. 5; guideline 1.2, p. 10
items.quote: refresh their risk management strategies accordingly
items.why: International comparator. Singapore's national guidance says AI brings attacks that ordinary IT does not, asks for threats and risks to be modelled, and tells system owners to keep up with developments in AI security and refresh their approach. Voluntary and deliberately non-prescriptive; no legal force in the UK.
